questions.explanation: Construct validity is a claim about what the numbers track, and the only way to support it is to show the numbers behave the way the construct should behave and not the way an unrelated quantity would. A stress task that moves the pulse and the scores together is evidence of the predicted kind; height and shoe size are unrelated things the scale should not follow. Stability over four weeks says the instrument is dependable, a panel's opinion says the items are on topic, and balanced wording makes the scoring cleaner. All three are useful, and none of them is evidence about the construct itself.

questions.explanation: The two requirements push in opposite directions, which is what makes them informative together. It is also cheap and it is not worthless: an instrument that offends a reader's sense of the construct will rarely perform well, and face validity is a useful screening step. questions.explanation: Internal consistency is a statement about the items among themselves: a person who scores high on one tends to score high on the others. answer.exemplar: The gap runs in one direction, and a consistent direction is not noise but a push towards what the respondent expects to be judged. Admiration for the organisation supplies a reason to look generous, and that reason operates on the reporting rather than on the volunteering, so the bias should grow exactly where the motive is strongest, which is what the data show. The administrative record does not share the motive, which is what makes the disagreement informative rather than a problem afflicting both sources. The fix is a design change: make every answer option equally creditable to somebody who wants to seem generous, or take the hours from the organisation rather than the person.

questions.explanation: Over-reporting in a consistent direction is not random error; it is the response moving towards the answer the respondent thinks is acceptable. An administrative record carries no such motive, which is what makes the disagreement between the two sources informative. The remedy is a design one: equalise how acceptable the answer options are, or take the count from the organisation rather than from the person.

answer.exemplar: Registration buys credibility by fixing the analysis before the data are seen, and the whole value of that commitment rests on the analysis being the one that was fixed. Switching away from it after seeing which version looks better reintroduces exactly the choice the registration was meant to close, and the number that results is no more protected than one from a study that was never registered at all. There is a legitimate way to handle this: report the registered analysis as the primary result, show the deviation with its reason, and present the alternative as the exploratory finding it has become. Transparency about the change repairs the reporting, and it does not repair the claim to have tested something in advance.

questions.explanation: The point of registering an analysis is that it cannot afterwards be chosen for what it shows, and an unregistered analysis is exactly what the scheme exists to rule out. Switching after seeing that the adjustment weakens the result puts the choice back in the researcher's hands, so the reported number carries no more protection than one from a study that was never registered. The proper response is to report the registered analysis as primary, state plainly what was changed and why, and label the deviation as exploratory. Being open about the change is what keeps the registration worth having.
questions.hint: Registration fixes the analysis, not the reporting of it.
questions.learningObjective: explain the status of a deviating analysis

answer.exemplar: Three outcomes, two comparison groupings, two time horizons and two missing-data rules give twenty-four combinations before anyone adds an outlier rule or a covariate set, and each combination is a defensible reading of the same data. The reported p-value is the smallest of those twenty-four, and a small number selected as the minimum of twenty-four is not distributed the way a single pre-specified p-value is; it sits much closer to zero than its face suggests. Nothing about the analysis is fraudulent, and every step is one a careful researcher would consider. The difficulty is structural, which is why the fix is a commitment made before the data rather than an extra caveat added afterwards.

questions.explanation: Those four choices multiply out to twenty-four analyses, all of them readable off the same data, and the reported p-value is whichever came out smallest. A minimum taken over twenty-four attempts is not distributed like a single planned p-value: it is much further towards zero than its own number implies, purely because it was selected. Nothing here is dishonest and every choice is one a careful researcher might defend, which is exactly why the problem is structural. The remedy is to commit to the analysis before seeing the data, or to report the whole family and the correction, rather than to add a caveat afterwards.
questions.hint: A reported p-value that was chosen as the smallest of many is not a single p-value.

questions.explanation: A mean near the bottom of the scale means almost everybody chose the lowest category, and a scale whose floor has been reached cannot register a further decrease. Any real difference between the two versions has to show up in a direction the item has no room for, so the comparison is between two piles of identical answers. Adding categories at the easy end, or replacing the item with one that can vary, restores the resolution. No choice of summary statistic recovers what the item itself has lost.
questions.hint: Where the mass of the responses sits tells you which end has run out of room.
questions.learningObjective: read a floor effect in a rating item

options.text: It pushes responses to the easy end, so a real difference in difficulty has almost nowhere to be recorded
It makes the versions indistinguishable, since no difference can appear where the scale has no room
options.misconception: concludes a null difference from the bunching

options.text: It shows the task is genuinely easy, which is a useful conclusion about the versions
options.misconception: reads the bunching as a substantive finding

options.text: It requires the analysis to use a median, since a mean is not appropriate on a five-point scale
options.misconception: prescribes a summary statistic instead of a design change

questions.explanation: Negative word use is itself a measure of negative affect, and a decent one, so a 0.62 correlation is close to what two related measures with ordinary amounts of error would produce. The study has shown convergence with one particular measure of something related, which is worth having and is not the same as evidence for the claimed construct. What is missing is anything that discriminates: a claim that the inventory does not respond to a different but related construct, and a structural account of what the thirty items are actually reporting. Without those, the criterion validates the mood, not the inventory's reading of it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the criterion might be measuring the same thing by a different route.

questions.explanation: Error in a predictor scatters each point either side of the true value, and the least-squares line through a scattered predictor is systematically flatter than the line through the true one. Nothing is compensated elsewhere in the model, so the estimate is biased downwards, and the amount of the loss is the predictor's reliability: 2.0 times 0.75 is 1.5, exactly what was reported. The same logic makes any model that also includes a second, correlated predictor look as though it has found a strong effect for that second predictor alone.
questions.hint: Scattering the predictor flattens the line; the reliability says by how much.
questions.learningObjective: state the direction of measurement-error bias and its size

options.text: Towards zero, and the slope retains exactly the reliability fraction of the error-free slope
Away from zero, and the slope exceeds the error-free slope by the same reliability fraction
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the bias

options.text: Unchanged, and the two slopes agree because the error is confined to the outcome variable
options.misconception: assumes the error sits in the outcome

options.text: Unchanged in size but shifted in sign, and the reliability fraction gives the shift directly
options.misconception: invents a sign change that the model does not produce

questions.explanation: The design works because a household scoring 49.9 and one scoring 50.1 are on the same side of everything that matters except luck, so any difference between them can only be the rule. That is a claim about the counterfactual at the threshold, and the only evidence for it is how the two groups compare below the line, where no support is given. If outcomes were already on a different path on the two sides, the design has found a difference without a cause, and a density check for households bunching just above the line is what looks for exactly that manipulation.
questions.hint: The argument is about similarity near the line, and only the data below it can show it.

That the thresholds were set at random, so the comparison needs no further support

options.text: That no household can move across the line, so the two groups are certainly different people
options.misconception: relies on the opposite of what the design needs

options.text: That the outcome is recorded after the award, so the timing alone establishes the direction

answer.exemplar: Predicting repeat purchases is a genuine achievement, and it is achieved by measuring whatever drives them, which need not be the feeling the developers had in mind. A scale that captured how customers are likely to behave would predict just as well while telling you nothing at all about how they feel, and nothing in the predictive record can tell those two instruments apart. That is the structural limit of criterion evidence: it establishes usefulness, and usefulness is compatible with several quite different underlying accounts of what is being measured. Discriminant evidence and a structural account of the items are what would support the construct claim, and neither can be replaced by a good correlation with an outcome.

questions.explanation: The scale predicts something real, and predicting it well is what makes the scale useful rather than what makes it a measure of satisfaction. A scale capturing how customers are likely to behave would predict repeat purchases just as successfully while knowing nothing about their feelings, and the predictive record gives a reader no way to tell those two instruments apart. Criterion evidence is evidence of usefulness, and usefulness is compatible with several different accounts of what is being measured. Discriminant evidence, and some account of what the items are actually reporting, are what would support a construct claim, and no correlation with an outcome can stand in for them.
questions.hint: Predicting a real outcome well is compatible with measuring something other than the claim.
questions.learningObjective: explain how an instrument can be right and the construct wrong

answer.exemplar: A correlation between two measurements is held down by the error in each, and an instrument that is nearly half noise cannot display a relationship it actually has. Raising the reliability removes that ceiling, so the observed movement is exactly what attenuation predicts and nothing more: the same underlying relationship, read through a clearer copy of the same items. A reader who treats the gain as a change in the world will believe the construct has become better related to the criterion, when what has happened is that the instrument has stopped obscuring it. This is why any validation study reports the reliabilities of both instruments, since a correlation quoted without them cannot be read at all.

questions.explanation: The items were not rewritten, so the underlying relationship between the two constructs is the same one it was before. What changed is how clearly the scale reads it, and a correlation is limited from above by the error in the two measurements, so removing error raises the observed value without changing the world. 0.28 is what a relationship of this size looks like through a 0.55 reliable instrument, and 0.51 is what it looks like through a 0.88 reliable one. This is why a validation report has to quote the reliabilities: without them the correlation cannot be interpreted at all, and nobody can tell a clearer instrument from a stronger relationship.
questions.hint: The two figures may describe the same relationship seen through different quality instruments.
questions.learningObjective: explain the validity ceiling created by unreliability

answer.exemplar: People lean towards the agreeable answer, and they do not lean towards it in a way that distinguishes the two wordings, so a positively worded item collects that tendency and a negatively worded one collects it against itself. The two sets of items are therefore measuring the response style as much as the attitude, and in opposite directions, which is why combining them into a single score can cancel the attitude out entirely. Reversing the wording of half the items, as balanced designs do, is the standard remedy, and it works only if the balance is built in from the start rather than added after the data arrive.

questions.explanation: A shared tendency to agree, unrelated to the attitude being asked about, is being recorded by one wording and subtracted by the other. That is why the two sets disagree so sharply while the attitudes behind them do not, and it is why summing the two sets can cancel the very thing the battery was built to measure. Wording half the items in the opposite direction and reversing the scores is the standard remedy, so that the tendency enters both halves with the same sign and drops out of the total. Adding the reversal after the fact is not the same thing: it changes the score without changing what was collected.
questions.hint: A tendency to agree enters one wording positively and the other negatively.
questions.learningObjective: explain how acquiescence appears in item data

questions.explanation: The definition comes first because every later decision, from wording to scoring to what counts as adequate evidence, is judged against it, and a vague definition is the usual reason an instrument ends up measuring something else. Item writing and expert review follow, and they are the point at which the content claim is either supported or exposed. Piloting catches what experts miss, chiefly whether respondents read an item the way it was meant. Reliability is estimated after the scoring has settled rather than before, because a coefficient for a set of items measures the set as scored. The validity evidence comes last, and it is the part that never finishes.
questions.hint: Every later decision is judged against the first one.
questions.learningObjective: sequence the development of a measurement instrument

Draft items, review them against the domain, and put them to expert judges for coverage
Pilot the items on a small group and remove or rewrite whatever the responses expose
Estimate the reliability of the chosen scoring in a full sample, and check the reliabilities it needs
Gather convergent and discriminant evidence against outside measures, and report what it does not show

questions.explanation: The nesting has to be described first, because the group sizes decide how much each level's variance can be estimated from and a badly sized level produces a variance that is mostly guesswork. Deciding which levels vary comes next, since a level modelled as fixed when it is really a sample of something will have its variance silently absorbed elsewhere. The variance estimates are inspected before the programme effect, because a treatment estimate is uninterpretable while the levels above and below it remain undescribed. The programme's own level is then checked against the level of randomisation, since a programme delivered to whole schools cannot be separated from school differences otherwise.
questions.hint: Nothing about the effect means much until the variances around it are known.

Fit the model and inspect each estimated variance before reading any treatment effect
Check the programme's own level against the level at which it was randomised
Report how much of the outcome variation each level accounts for, alongside the effect

questions.explanation: The threshold, outcome and window are fixed before anything is fitted, because a window chosen after seeing the plot can be trimmed until it flatters the result. The plot is the honest first look, and it says whether there is any jump to estimate and whether the points are dense near the line. Estimation follows, and then the specification checks, which are where a small result usually turns out to be an artefact of one particular window. The density examination belongs at the end but is the most important of the five: households who sort themselves across a threshold show up as a spike, and a discontinuity estimated on a manipulated sample describes the sorting rather than the rule.
questions.hint: Everything is fixed before fitting, and the manipulation check is the one that can void the result.

options.text: Fix the threshold, the outcome and the window either side of it before fitting anything
Plot the outcome against the running variable and look for a jump at the line
Fit a model on each side and estimate the size of the discontinuity at the line
Vary the window, the order of the polynomial and the estimator to see what the result depends on
Examine the density of observations either side, since a spike reveals people sorting themselves

questions.explanation: The structure comes first, because what counts as a confounder depends on it, and a variable that confounds one structure may be harmless in another. The effect and its interval are then stated on the outcome's own scale, since a threshold expressed as an odds ratio is harder to reason about than one expressed in the units people care about. The threshold strength is computed next, and it is a symmetrical requirement, so a confounder would have to be associated with exposure and outcome to the same degree. The second part is the one reviewers skip: checking whether the adjusted confounders are themselves associated with exposure tells you whether anything was adjusted for that should not have been, which often undermines the estimate more than an unmeasured one would.
questions.hint: What counts as a confounder depends on the structure, and the structure is written first.
questions.learningObjective: sequence a sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding

options.text: Write the causal structure and name the variables that could plausibly act as confounders

Compute the strength an unmeasured confounder would need on both the exposure and outcome sides
Ask whether the confounders actually adjusted for are themselves associated with the exposure
Say what would change the answer, and what evidence would have to be collected to find out
